step1_summary.Chief complaint: Recent onset of breathlessness and right-sided back pain on deep inspiration lasting about a day.
Symptoms: Pain on deep breaths, localized to right-hand side of back
Slight fever (felt warm, no measured temp)
Two episodes of coughing up blood (hemoptysis)
Palpitations or sensation of increased heart rate
Tiredness and decreased exercise tolerance for 2 weeks
No recent long-haul flights or known clots
step1_summary.Medications/allergies: Methotrexate (taken this morning), no medication allergies
step1_summary.Family/social history: No family history of blood clots; non-smoker; office worker; lives alone with a cat
step1_summary.Vital signs/exam findings: Heart rate approx. 66-74 bpm (normal), no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy, good peripheral circulation, limited virtual exam
step1_summary.Labs/imaging: None yet performed; possible follow-up chest X-ray suggested

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute onset pleuritic pain, breathlessness, hemoptysis, and palpitations with normal HR suggests a clot in lung circulation.
Pneumonia with pleuritis: Fever, cough with blood, pleuritic pain, and recent illness suggest chest infection causing inflammation and bleeding.
Pulmonary vasculitis: SLE patient might develop small vessel vasculitis causing lung hemorrhage and pleuritic pain.
I: Pneumonia: Fever, cough with blood, pleuritic chest pain and overall recent symptoms consistent with lung infection.
Lung abscess or tuberculosis: Hemoptysis and fever could be infectious but less likely acute onset.
N: Lung cancer: Hemoptysis and pleuritic pain; less likely given abrupt onset and age but requires exclusion given symptoms.
Mediastinal lymphoma: Can cause cough and hemoptysis but usually more insidious.
D: Anemia or chronic disease fatigue: Explains tiredness but not acute symptoms.
Interstitial lung disease: SLE can cause this but less likely acute with hemoptysis.
I2: Methotrexate lung toxicity: Methotrexate can cause pneumonitis or pulmonary fibrosis but usually more subacute to chronic.
Drug-induced bleeding: Methotrexate is unlikely to cause hemoptysis directly, but consider.
C: Congenital heart disease with pulmonary hypertension causing hemoptysis: Unlikely given age and no history.
A: SLE-related pulmonary hemorrhage or lupus pneumonitis: Possible given history of SLE and acute hemoptysis with fever.
Allergic pneumonitis: Less likely with current presentation.
T: Trauma to chest causing bleeding and pain: No history of trauma, unlikely.
E: Anemia of chronic disease causing fatigue: Explains fatigue but not main acute symptoms.
Thromboembolic disease secondary to lupus anticoagulant syndrome: SLE patients can develop coagulopathy leading to clots.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset fever, pleuritic pain, cough with hemoptysis, and tiredness are all classical features. SLE can predispose to infections. Examination findings and clinical context support this diagnosis.
opposing_evidence: Normal pulse and vitals during virtual exam

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and breathlessness are suggestive, although no history of venous clots or long flights. SLE patients have increased risk of thromboembolism. Normal heart rate argues against severe embolism but cannot exclude.
supporting_evidence: Acute pleuritic chest pain localized to the back
opposing_evidence: No prior history of clots or family history
No swelling or leg pain reported

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: SLE-related pulmonary hemorrhage or lupus pneumonitis (Autoimmune)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Known SLE patient on immunomodulator therapy presenting with fever, hemoptysis, and pleuritic pain; lupus pneumonitis and pulmonary hemorrhage are recognized manifestations and could explain symptoms.
supporting_evidence: Hemoptysis and pleuritic pain with fever
Recent fatigue consistent with SLE flare
opposing_evidence: No prior SLE lung involvement reported
No other systemic flare symptoms described
Normal oxygenation and pulse rate not documented

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Hemoptysis and pain could be caused by cancer, but the acute onset, absence of weight loss or chronic symptoms, and patient's age reduce likelihood. Still requires exclusion.
opposing_evidence: No weight loss or chronic systemic symptoms
